blocks.content: Mizoram's culture chapter is anchored by its distinctive bamboo dance (Cheraw), its modern Christian-influenced festival calendar, and a genuinely strong claim to having one of India's highest literacy-driven, community-oriented civic cultures.

Cheraw, popularly known as the 'Bamboo Dance', is Mizoram's most iconic and internationally recognised traditional dance form, in which dancers (typically women) step rhythmically in and out of a grid of horizontal bamboo poles, which are simultaneously clapped open and shut in coordinated rhythm by seated performers — requiring exceptional precision and timing.

Cheraw is believed to be one of the oldest Mizo traditional dance forms, historically associated with funerary/ancestral rites in pre-Christian Mizo tradition, though it is performed today primarily as a celebratory cultural showcase at festivals and public events, including the annual Chapchar Kut festival (below).

★ EXAM POINT: Cheraw ('Bamboo Dance') is Mizoram's single most iconic and frequently tested cultural-dance fact — remember its distinctive technique (dancers stepping between rhythmically clapped bamboo poles) and its historical association with pre-Christian funerary rites.

cells: Mizoram's most important and widely celebrated festival, a spring festival marking the completion of jhum (shifting cultivation) jungle-clearing; features Cheraw and other traditional dances, feasting and community celebration
Maize-harvest festival, traditionally including remembrance of deceased family members
Post-harvest thanksgiving festival, marking the end of the agricultural cycle
Widely and centrally celebrated, given Mizoram's overwhelmingly Christian population (Chapter 7)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Chapchar Kut, Mim Kut and Pawl Kut are Mizoram's traditional 'Kut' (festival) cycle, each tied to a specific stage of the jhum cultivation agricultural calendar (jungle-clearing, maize harvest, and post-harvest respectively) — Chapchar Kut is by far the most prominent and widely celebrated of the three.

Reflecting the strong influence of Christian church institutions (Chapter 7), Mizoram has a distinctive history of social-reform-driven alcohol regulation — the state enforced total prohibition of alcohol under the Mizoram Liquor Total Prohibition Act for an extended period (from the late 1990s), before liberalising this policy to a regulated, permit-based sale system in more recent years; the state also maintains an active, church-and-civil-society-supported anti-drug/anti-substance-abuse campaign, given Mizoram's geographic proximity to the Golden Triangle drug-trafficking region via the Myanmar border.

Chapchar Kut (spring) = most important festival; Mim Kut (autumn) and Pawl Kut (winter) complete the traditional 'Kut' festival cycle tied to the jhum agricultural calendar.
